Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Kofi had always been a man of routine and precision, but since fleeing his war-torn homeland at the age of 55, he found himself increasingly withdrawn. The sound of authority figures giving commands transported him back to the day he was forced to leave his village under threat from rebels. The memories of that fateful event were fragmented, consisting mainly of vivid images: the burning huts, the screaming children, and the faces of the armed men who had ordered them to evacuate. These snapshot memories haunted him, often triggered by mundane events like being given instructions at work or encountering someone in uniform. As Kofi's anxiety grew, he began to avoid going out, fearing that the sights and sounds of the city would overwhelm him. He stopped attending social gatherings with his wife, preferring to stay home and occupy himself with coding projects. His wife tried to be understanding, but Kofi could sense her growing frustration. At work, he became increasingly isolated, avoiding interactions with colleagues and taking extended breaks in the bathroom to collect his thoughts. But even these avoidance strategies couldn't keep the memories at bay. Sometimes, while working on a project, Kofi would feel detached and unreal, as if observing himself from outside his body. This dissociative feeling was always accompanied by vivid visual memories of the trauma, which he tried to push away by keeping his mind occupied all the time. He would work late into the night, often forgetting to eat or sleep, just to keep the images at bay. As Kofi's mental distraction tactics took a toll on his physical health, his doctor recommended that he take a break and focus on self-care. But for Kofi, avoiding people and going out was no longer just about managing anxiety; it had become a way of preserving his sanity. He feared that if he let his guard down, the memories would flood back, and he wouldn't be able to cope. The cycle of avoidance and rumination continued, with each component feeding into the others. The more Kofi avoided people and situations, the more he relied on mental distraction to calm himself, which in turn made it harder for him to recall his memories in a coherent narrative. And yet, the memories remained, frozen in time like snapshots, waiting to be triggered by some unexpected sound or image. Kofi's wife eventually convinced him to seek help, worried that his withdrawal would consume their relationship entirely. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kofi knew it was time to confront the past and break free from the cycle of avoidance and rumination that had held him hostage for so long. But what frightened him most was the prospect of reliving those memories, of being transported back to a place where he felt completely numb and detached.
